headline: QuickFee CEO highlights countercyclical demand tailwind, strong balance sheet capacity, and deep Xero integration as moat drivers
reasoning: Bruce Coombes notes that QuickFee's business is somewhat countercyclical, as tougher economic conditions drive more clients to seek professional advice from accountants and lawyers who in turn use QuickFee's financing solution. The company has a senior debt facility that funds 95% of originations, meaning QuickFee only needs to fund 5% from its own balance sheet, leaving significant capacity for inorganic growth using retained profits. The deep integration with Xero accounting software creates strong customer stickiness, as unwinding that integration would be a step backwards for clients. The company is paying a $0.01 per year dividend and considers this sustainable at current profit levels. While competitors could theoretically enter the space, Coombes argues the moat lies in deep understanding of how accountants and lawyers operate, particularly in the US market.
quote: The quick fee business is a little countercyclical, inasmuch as when times are a bit tougher, people need businesses, need a bit more advice from their accountant lawyer and have less capacity to pay for it. So that's a little bit of a tailwind on the quick fee business... we've got a senior debt facility which supports 95% of originations. So we only need to fund 5% of what we originate in terms of our loan book. So our capacity to do something inorganic using profits and retained earnings and our strong balance sheet is very real... we have a deep integration with the Xero accounting software platform in Australia... Once they've got that deep integration, which goes both ways right through to receding back into their zero system, it's it would be a step backwards to lead quickly.
episode_title: QuickFee gets back to basics, and he profits are following

headline: Posts maiden full-year profit and initiates dividend after simplifying to core lending business in AU and US
reasoning: QuickFee sold its US card/EFT processing and software businesses for ~A$40m, returned capital to shareholders, and is now entirely focused on its low-risk B2B lending solution for accounting and legal professionals. The company achieved its first full-year profit, paid an interim dividend, and published FY27 EBITDA guidance of ~$5m at the midpoint. Growth is expected from late-FY26 customer signings ramping up plus new client acquisition via US distributor Iwan, which serves 300 of the top 500 CPA firms. The business model is described as countercyclical and low-risk because the professional services firm stands behind every loan, providing higher yields with lower credit risk than typical SME lenders. The board intends to pay $0.01 per share annually (two half-cent dividends) as long as current profitability is sustained.
quote: The sale of two of the three businesses we were operating in the United States. The two we sold were our card and EFT processing business, as well as our software business. And we were fortunate enough to receive 40 million AUD for those as a result, not needed to simplify our business. It gave us the opportunity to pay money back to our shareholders by way of capital return, and focus entirely on running our low risk lending business in Australia and the US. So profitable first dividend capital returns.
episode_title: QuickFee gets back to basics, and he profits are following
